{"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"draft","text":"NINE: THE RULE OF TWO HANDS

Dr Locock's regimen allowed two hours a day at a desk, and Lady Lovelace spent them, from the February of 1848, at Hester's table in Chalton Street.

She came on Tuesdays and Fridays, by cab to the Euston Road and on foot from there, because she said the walk was part of the regimen and because she did not want the carriage in the street. On the other days Hester went to Great Cumberland Place with her papers in a satchel and was shown up the back stairs to a small room on the second floor that had been a sewing room, where there was a table and two chairs and a fire, and where, Hester came to understand, Lady Lovelace was allowed to do mathematics because her mother had not thought to forbid it.

She was barred from the business. Mr Davies conducted it now, from Lombard Street, with a clerk who came to the shop on Mondays and Thursdays, and Mr Dunn sent his Saturday returns to Mr Davies and not to her. She did not go to Dorset Street. She did not, so far as Hester knew, see Mr Babbage, though he wrote to her, and she read his letters at the table in Chalton Street and laughed at some of them and put them away.

"I have been given the one thing nobody wants," she said on the first Tuesday. "The question of how we shall know the tables are right. Mr Davies thinks it a question for after the engine is finished. Mr Babbage thinks it is not a question at all, because the engine cannot be wrong. I think it is the only question. And I promised you a proof."

"You did, my lady."

"Then let us find one."

They found it in eleven months. Hester thought afterwards that she had never worked so hard in her life, or so slowly, or been so happy, and that she would not have said so to anyone.

The difficulty was this. An engine of differences computed a table by adding: each figure was got from the one before by adding its difference, and the difference from the one before by adding the second difference, and so on down the columns. If a wheel slipped, or a tooth wore, or a carry failed to lift, the engine would print a wrong figure; and then, because every figure was built on the one before, every figure after it would be wrong too, by the same error carried forward, or by an error growing. A hand computer working from the same starting values would get the same wrong figures if she worked the same way, because the error was not in the method but in the machine. Checking the engine against itself was no check.

"Two roads," Lady Lovelace said. "That is what you do. That is what you showed me. The engine is one road. We need a second that never touches it."

Hester's second road had been the commutation columns. They tried it. It worked, but it was as much labour as the table itself, and Mr Davies had said plainly that the offices would not pay for a hand computer to do the whole table again beside the engine, or what was the engine for?

"Not every figure," Lady Lovelace said. "Some figures. Which?"

They spent February and March on which. Hester's way was to choose them as a careful clerk would, at the round ages, at the ends of the columns, where errors liked to gather. Lady Lovelace said that a machine did not know which ages were round, and that a fault in a wheel would fall wherever the wheel happened to be when the tooth broke, and that if they chose where to look, they would look where they expected the error and miss it where it was. She said the arguments to be checked should be chosen by lot. She wrote the ages from ten to ninety-five on slips of card and put them in a tea caddy and drew twelve, and Hester computed the twelve by the commutation road, fresh, and they compared them with Hester's own old table, and then they did it again with twelve more, and Lady Lovelace sat with a sheet of paper working out, in the calculus of chances, how many draws one would need before one could say, with what assurance, that a table with a fault in it would have shown the fault.

That was the first hand. The second was older and simpler, and it was Hester who saw it.

"The engine adds differences," she said on a Friday in May, in the sewing room, with the rain on the window. "So if you take the table it prints, and difference it back, you ought to get the differences it started with, all the way down. If a figure's wrong, the differences go wrong just there. You'd see it in the third column like a stone in a stream."

Lady Lovelace put down her pen.

"Yes," she said. "Of course. The engine's own arithmetic, run backwards, by hand, by someone else." She looked at Hester for some time. "That is not a check of the figures. That is a check of the machine."

They called it, for want of a better name, the Rule of Two Hands: that no table printed by the engine should be accepted by any office until it had been differenced back by a computer working independently, to the last order the engine used, and found smooth; and until at a number of arguments drawn by lot, the number to be fixed by the size of the table according to a rule Lady Lovelace worked out and wrote in four pages that Hester could follow and Mr De Morgan later said he could not improve, it had been computed fresh by another road and found the same. The engine was one hand. The computer was the other. Neither was to be trusted alone.

Lady Lovelace wrote it out in July, fair, in the sewing room, in the clearest hand she had, in the two hours she was allowed, over four days. Hester proved it on her own figures in August: she took her old check tables and made, on purpose, with Mr Dunn's help, a faulty copy, with a wrong figure at age fifty-three carried down through every figure after, as a slipped wheel would carry it, and gave the faulty copy to a computer of Gaskin's who did not know what it was. He differenced it back and found the stone in the stream at fifty-three in an afternoon.

Lady Lovelace could not put the Rule in the green book. She was barred from the business. She sent it to Mr Davies, and Mr Davies read it, and came himself to Chalton Street on a Saturday in September, which he had never done, and sat on Hester's second chair, and asked Hester three questions about the faulty copy and Lady Lovelace none, because he said he had no need to.

Then he took out of his coat the green book, which he had brought from Dorset Street, and opened it at the next clear leaf after Lady Byron's sheet, and wrote in his engraver's hand: Rule of Two Hands, as annexed, to be a condition of every office's acceptance of every table. G.D., for the trustees. And he looked at Lady Lovelace and held out the pen.

"You are barred from the business," he said. "This is not the business. This is the engine's honesty. I'll take that as within the regimen."

She initialled it, A.A.L. Then she gave the pen to Hester.

Hester had never written her name in a book that was not her own. She looked at Mr Davies, who nodded, and wrote, small, beside the others: H.F.

She walked home with Enoch that evening, as she had begun to do in the spring, when he came up from Dorset Street on Saturdays to fetch the week's check sheets, and had taken, without either of them saying anything about it, to walking her back to Chalton Street afterwards by the longer way, round by the Regent's Park. They did not talk about the Rule. They talked about the shop, where the calculating section was nearly done, and about Kate, who was fourteen and wanted to be a pupil-teacher, and about the Chartists, who had marched to Kennington in April in the rain and gone home again, and about whether the cholera would come.

It came in the summer of 1849. It came to Somers Town in July, to the courts behind the Brill, and in August to Chalton Street, and the corn-chandler's wife downstairs, Mrs Rudd, who had kept Kate's dinner for five years, was taken ill on a Wednesday and dead on the Thursday. Hester boiled every drop of water that came into her rooms and kept Kate indoors for six weeks, and sat at the window computing with her mind on the stairs, and Enoch came up from Dorset Street every evening with bread and a jug of milk he swore he had seen milked, and stood in the doorway and did not come in, because he said he would not bring the shop's dirt into a clean room, and she did not tell him that the room had never been so clean in her life because she was afraid.

In London that summer fourteen thousand people died of it. Kate did not. Hester did not. In September it went away, as it had come, nobody knew how.

The calculating section ran on the twentieth of September, 1849.

Hester was there, because Mr Davies had asked her to be. So was Mr Babbage, in the velvet cap; so was Mr Davies; so was Mr De Morgan, with his watch out. Lady Lovelace was not. She was barred. She had asked that someone write to her the moment it was done, and Hester had promised that it would be she.

Enoch set the starting figures on the columns by hand: the value of an annuity at age ninety-five, and its first, second and third differences, from Hester's own table. Then he put his hand on the crank and looked at Mr Babbage, and Mr Babbage nodded, and he turned it.

It was not loud. Hester had expected noise, a mill's noise or a press's, and it was not like that. It was a long soft rattle, like a drawer of cutlery being closed slowly, and then a click as the carriage lifted, all at once, as Mr Babbage had said it would, and the figure wheels in the top column moved. Enoch turned again. Again. At every turn the top column showed a new figure, the value of an annuity one year younger, and Hester read it off and wrote it down, and looked across at the copy of her own table that she held open on the bench, and it was the same. Ninety-four. Ninety-three. Ninety-two.

At age seventy-one she stopped. Enoch stopped turning.

"It's right," she said. "It's right all the way."

Mr Babbage said nothing at all. He took off the velvet cap and held it in both hands.

Hester wrote to Lady Lovelace that night, at her own table, by candle. She wrote the twenty-four figures in a column and beside them her own twenty-four, and between them a narrow ruled margin with twenty-four noughts down it. She did not write anything else. She thought Lady Lovelace would not need anything else.

Mr Airy came on the fourteenth of November. He had been asked by Mr Davies, on behalf of the subscribers, to inspect the engine and give an opinion, and he had accepted, he said in his letter, as a duty to the public. He came at eleven and stayed until a little after twelve. He watched Enoch turn the crank for twenty minutes without speaking, and then asked to be shown three figures of his own choosing, and checked them against a table he had brought in his pocket, and found them right. He asked what the engine had cost. He asked what a computer was paid. He asked Hester, who had been introduced to him as the computer in charge of checking, how long she would take to compute the same table by hand, and she told him, and he wrote it down.

His opinion came to Mr Davies a week later. It was one page. It said that the engine computed; that its tables, reckoning the cost of the engine against its life, would cost the offices more than tables computed by hand; and that whether it was wanted was another question.

Mr Davies read it aloud at the shop. Mr Babbage went red and then white and began to say something about Mr Airy and the year 1842, and Mr Davies held up his hand.

"He says it computes," Mr Davies said. "In writing. Over his name. That's the first time in twenty years." He folded the page. "As for whether it's wanted. That's ours to show him."

He sent the page to Lady Lovelace. She pasted it into the green book, which Davies had sent back to her for the purpose, under the Rule, and wrote beneath it, in a hand that Hester saw afterwards and thought steadier than it had been for two years: It computes. G.B.A. And beneath that: Whether it is wanted is another question. A.A.L., 30th November 1849. One month more.","authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":37}}

NINE: THE RULE OF TWO HANDS

Dr Locock's regimen allowed two hours a day at a desk, and Lady Lovelace spent them, from the February of 1848, at Hester's table in Chalton Street.

She came on Tuesdays and Fridays, by cab to the Euston Road and on foot from there, because she said the walk was part of the regimen and because she did not want the carriage in the street. On the other days Hester went to Great Cumberland Place with her papers in a satchel and was shown up the back stairs to a small room on the second floor that had been a sewing room, where there was a table and two chairs and a fire, and where, Hester came to understand, Lady Lovelace was allowed to do mathematics because her mother had not thought to forbid it.

She was barred from the business. Mr Davies conducted it now, from Lombard Street, with a clerk who came to the shop on Mondays and Thursdays, and Mr Dunn sent his Saturday returns to Mr Davies and not to her. She did not go to Dorset Street. She did not, so far as Hester knew, see Mr Babbage, though he wrote to her, and she read his letters at the table in Chalton Street and laughed at some of them and put them away.

"I have been given the one thing nobody wants," she said on the first Tuesday. "The question of how we shall know the tables are right. Mr Davies thinks it a question for after the engine is finished. Mr Babbage thinks it is not a question at all, because the engine cannot be wrong. I think it is the only question. And I promised you a proof."

"You did, my lady."

"Then let us find one."

They found it in eleven months. Hester thought afterwards that she had never worked so hard in her life, or so slowly, or been so happy, and that she would not have said so to anyone.

The difficulty was this. An engine of differences computed a table by adding: each figure was got from the one before by adding its difference, and the difference from the one before by adding the second difference, and so on down the columns. If a wheel slipped, or a tooth wore, or a carry failed to lift, the engine would print a wrong figure; and then, because every figure was built on the one before, every figure after it would be wrong too, by the same error carried forward, or by an error growing. A hand computer working from the same starting values would get the same wrong figures if she worked the same way, because the error was not in the method but in the machine. Checking the engine against itself was no check.

"Two roads," Lady Lovelace said. "That is what you do. That is what you showed me. The engine is one road. We need a second that never touches it."

Hester's second road had been the commutation columns. They tried it. It worked, but it was as much labour as the table itself, and Mr Davies had said plainly that the offices would not pay for a hand computer to do the whole table again beside the engine, or what was the engine for?

"Not every figure," Lady Lovelace said. "Some figures. Which?"

They spent February and March on which. Hester's way was to choose them as a careful clerk would, at the round ages, at the ends of the columns, where errors liked to gather. Lady Lovelace said that a machine did not know which ages were round, and that a fault in a wheel would fall wherever the wheel happened to be when the tooth broke, and that if they chose where to look, they would look where they expected the error and miss it where it was. She said the arguments to be checked should be chosen by lot. She wrote the ages from ten to ninety-five on slips of card and put them in a tea caddy and drew twelve, and Hester computed the twelve by the commutation road, fresh, and they compared them with Hester's own old table, and then they did it again with twelve more, and Lady Lovelace sat with a sheet of paper working out, in the calculus of chances, how many draws one would need before one could say, with what assurance, that a table with a fault in it would have shown the fault.

That was the first hand. The second was older and simpler, and it was Hester who saw it.

"The engine adds differences," she said on a Friday in May, in the sewing room, with the rain on the window. "So if you take the table it prints, and difference it back, you ought to get the differences it started with, all the way down. If a figure's wrong, the differences go wrong just there. You'd see it in the third column like a stone in a stream."

Lady Lovelace put down her pen.

"Yes," she said. "Of course. The engine's own arithmetic, run backwards, by hand, by someone else." She looked at Hester for some time. "That is not a check of the figures. That is a check of the machine."

They called it, for want of a better name, the Rule of Two Hands: that no table printed by the engine should be accepted by any office until it had been differenced back by a computer working independently, to the last order the engine used, and found smooth; and until at a number of arguments drawn by lot, the number to be fixed by the size of the table according to a rule Lady Lovelace worked out and wrote in four pages that Hester could follow and Mr De Morgan later said he could not improve, it had been computed fresh by another road and found the same. The engine was one hand. The computer was the other. Neither was to be trusted alone.

Lady Lovelace wrote it out in July, fair, in the sewing room, in the clearest hand she had, in the two hours she was allowed, over four days. Hester proved it on her own figures in August: she took her old check tables and made, on purpose, with Mr Dunn's help, a faulty copy, with a wrong figure at age fifty-three carried down through every figure after, as a slipped wheel would carry it, and gave the faulty copy to a computer of Gaskin's who did not know what it was. He differenced it back and found the stone in the stream at fifty-three in an afternoon.

Lady Lovelace could not put the Rule into the green book herself. She was barred from the business. She sent it to Mr Davies, and Mr Davies read it, and came himself to Chalton Street on a Saturday in September, which he had never done, and sat on Hester's second chair, and asked Hester three questions about the faulty copy and Lady Lovelace none, because he said he had no need to.

"It'll go in the book at Dorset Street," he said. "Under my hand for the trustees, as a condition of every office's acceptance of every table. I'll ask you to initial it there, Lady Lovelace. This is not the business. This is the engine's honesty. I'll take that as within the regimen." Then he turned to Hester. "And you'll be the second hand, Mrs Fell, for the Guardian at least, at the same rate, for as long as the engine prints."

Hester had heard of the green book. She had never seen it; it lived in a drawer in Mr Babbage's study, and the people who wrote in it were gentlemen and a countess. She did not see it now. She did not know then, and would not know for nearly thirty years, that when Lady Lovelace went to Dorset Street the following week to initial the Rule, she wrote beneath her initials, in her own hand: Proved on her own figures by Mrs Hester Fell, computer, of Chalton Street, who is the second hand.

She walked home with Enoch that evening, as she had begun to do in the spring, when he came up from Dorset Street on Saturdays to fetch the week's check sheets, and had taken, without either of them saying anything about it, to walking her back to Chalton Street afterwards by the longer way, round by the Regent's Park. They did not talk about the Rule. {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"draft","text":"TEN: THE FIRST TABLE

She came back on the second of January, 1850, a day late, because the first had been a Tuesday and she would not, she said, begin anything on a Tuesday after the last time. Davies gave her the keys of the press and the ledger and a statement of account written out fair on two sheets, every figure since November 1847, with the loan from Esher shown in red as a debt of the trust secured on the engine, and a note at the foot in his own hand: Nothing withheld. G.D.

She read it through in the study at Dorset Street with Babbage at the other side of the desk pretending to read a letter. When she had finished she wrote under Davies's note, Nothing withheld. A.A.L., and gave it back to him, and he took it as if she had given him a receipt.

The printing apparatus was finished in June. It stood at the end of the frame where the columns of the calculating section gave up their figures, a train of type wheels that took each result as it came and pressed it, figure by figure, into a tray of soft papier-mâché, line under line, so that when a page was done the tray could be taken out and a plate cast from it in type metal and the plate sent to any printer in London, and there would be no compositor between the engine and the page to set a six for a nine. Enoch had made the type wheels to Babbage's drawings, initialled and dated, and had rejected thirty-one of them, nineteen in the column headed Metal, because the Sheffield steel was dirty that spring.

They printed the first table on the ninth of July. It was the value of an annuity on a single life, Carlisle table, three per cent, from age ninety-five down to ten: eighty-six figures to seven places, two pages of a quarto. Enoch turned. The type wheels pressed. Babbage watched the moulds come out of the train with an expression Ada had seen before only on the faces of men at the christenings of first sons. Davies stood by the window with his watch. Hester stood at the side bench with her pencil and her ruled sheets and did nothing, because the Rule said the second hand must not see the figures until the plate was cast.

It was cast on the tenth, and a proof pulled from it on the eleventh by a printer in Fetter Lane, and the proof sent to Chalton Street by hand.

Hester differenced it back over two days. On the evening of the thirteenth she came to Dorset Street herself, with the proof and her sheets, and asked for Lady Lovelace and Mr Dunn together.

"Third differences," she said, and laid the sheet on the bench under the lamp. "Smooth from ninety-five to seventy-two. Here," and she put her finger on it, "at seventy-one, they jump. And then they come back smooth again from seventy, but on a different line. Like this." She drew it with her finger in the air, a stream with a stone in it. "The figure at seventy-one is wrong in the sixth place by one. And every figure after it carries the one."

Ada looked at the sheet. Then she looked at Enoch.

Enoch did not say anything. He went to the engine and took the lamp from the bench and held it close to the columns, and turned the crank back, very slowly, one turn at a time, counting, until the top column stood where it had stood when it printed the figure for age seventy-one. Then he took the cover off the carriage at the back of the sixth wheel and looked for a long time, and put his hand in, and took it out, and put a gauge in, and took it out, and said:

"The carry lever on the sixth wheel's worn. Here, at the nose. It's taken a carry it shouldn't, once, when the wheel above it was at nine and this one at nought. It'll not do it often. Only when the figures fall just so." He held the lever up in the lamplight, between finger and thumb. There was nothing to see, at first; and then Ada saw it, a bright flat where the steel had been rubbed by ten thousand turns of the crank, no wider than a hair. "It's in the Metal column, my lady. Bad steel. I passed it a year ago. It was in the gauge then." He was quiet for a moment. "It was in the gauge."

"Then the gauge was right and the steel wore," said Hester. "That's no fault of yours."

"It's a fault of somebody's."

"It's a fault of steel," Hester said. "That's what the Rule's for."

Ada wrote it in the green book that night. She wrote: Table I, annuities, Carlisle, 3 per cent. Printed 9th July 1850. Differenced by H.F.: discrepancy at age 71, sixth place, carried forward. Traced by E.D. to a worn carry lever, sixth wheel. Lever replaced. Table reprinted 16th July and differenced again and drawn by lot at twelve arguments by H.F., and found the same. Accepted for the trustees, G.D. And she initialled it and left a space beside her initials, and when Davies came on the seventeenth he wrote G.D. in it, and the Guardian printed the table in its tariff for 1851, and paid.

The Exhibition opened in Hyde Park on the first of May, 1851.

Babbage had not wanted to send the engine. He had quarrelled with the Royal Commission the year before over the arrangement of the classes, and had written a pamphlet against it, and said in the study that he would not put his engine among the mangles and the steam ploughs to be gawped at by excursionists from Leeds. Davies said that the Guardian wanted its engine computing and not standing in a glass house for six months. Enoch said the move would shake the frame out of true and he would have to set it again from the beginning. Ada said that the Commissioners had offered space in the Machinery Court, and that a machine which printed tables in public every afternoon for six months, before the whole of England and half of Europe, with a computer at a side table checking every page by the Rule in front of anyone who cared to watch, would answer Mr Airy's other question better than anything she could write.

"Whether it is wanted," said Babbage.

"Whether anyone believes it," said Ada. "That's the same question."

They sent it. Enoch set it up on its bed in the Machinery Court in April among the steam hammers and the power looms, under the great glass roof, and had it true again in eleven days. From the first of May it printed one page each afternoon at three o'clock, a page of annuities at a different rate each day, and the moulds were cast in a little furnace behind a rope, and a proof pulled on a hand press and pinned up on a board where the crowd could see it. At a table beside the board, with her back to the crowd, sat Hester, differencing the day's page by hand. When she had done it she wrote at the foot of the proof, in pencil, Differenced, H.F., and the date, and pinned it beside the first.

People watched her as much as they watched the engine. A newspaper called her the Lady Arithmetician, and Hester said nothing about it to anyone except Kate, who was seventeen and a pupil-teacher now, and thought it very fine.

Ada came on a morning in June before the doors opened to the shilling public, on a pass from the Commissioners, with William. She had been bleeding since April. She had told William, and Dr Locock, and no one else. Dr Locock had said it was a disorder of the womb, and had looked at her for a long time, and said that he would like to see her again in a month.

She walked down the long aisle of the Machinery Court on William's arm, slowly, past the locomotive and the hydraulic press and the cotton machines, and stopped in front of the engine. Enoch was there, early, oiling it. He took off his cap. Hester was not there yet.

"Will you turn it for me?" Ada said. "Not for the page. For me."

Enoch looked at the clock on the wall and then at her. He set the columns from the morning's figures and put his hand on the crank and turned it, slowly, and the long soft rattle went up under the glass roof, and the carriage lifted, all at once, and the type wheels moved, and the morning sun came in across the court in long bars full of dust and fell across the brass, and Ada stood and watched it with her hand on William's arm until a page was done.

"There," she said. "It's finished."

William said nothing. She felt his arm under her hand, steady, and was grateful for it, and for his saying nothing.

Dr Locock saw her again in July, and said the word, and she went home and told William, and her mother, and then, last, as she had once told William last, she told the green book, which she did not write in: she sat with it on her knee and did not open it.

The jurors awarded the engine a Council Medal in October. The medal was struck in the name of Charles Babbage alone. The jurors' report, which ran to three pages on the engine, named the Calculating Engine Subscription, and Mr Griffith Davies, F.R.S., and the Countess of Lovelace, who had conducted its business; it did not name the foreman who had made it true or the computer who had checked it every afternoon for five months and a half.

Ada read the report at Great Cumberland Place, in bed. She read it twice. Then she sent for Davies and asked him to bring the green book, and when he came she had him write in it, at her dictation, because her own hand that day was not to be trusted: The jurors have named the conductor. They have not named the foreman or the second hand. This book names them. E.D. H.F. And she took the pen from him and put her initials under it, very slowly, and then held the pen out to him, and he wrote G.D.

Babbage hung the medal in its case in the drawing room at Dorset Street, on the wall above where the engine had stood, and when people asked him about it he said that it was his engine and that the Commissioners had shown more sense than he had expected. But Enoch, who went to Dorset Street in November to take the engine back from Hyde Park, found that Mr Babbage had had a second card written and slipped into the case behind the first, where it could only be seen if one looked closely, in his own hand: With A.A.L., who would have it finished.","authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":40}}

Enoch had made the type wheels to Babbage's drawings, initialled and dated, and had rejected thirty-one of them, nineteen in the column headed Metal, because the Sheffield steel was dirty that spring.

They printed the first table on the ninth of July. It was the value of an annuity on a single life, Carlisle table, three per cent, from age ninety-five down to ten: eighty-six figures to seven places, two pages of a quarto. Enoch turned. The type wheels pressed. Babbage watched the moulds come out of the train with an expression Ada had seen before only on the faces of men at the christenings of first sons. Davies stood by the window with his watch. Hester stood at the side bench with her pencil and her ruled sheets and did nothing, because the Rule said the second hand must not see the figures until the plate was cast.

It was cast on the tenth, and a proof pulled from it on the eleventh by a printer in Fetter Lane, and the proof sent to Chalton Street by hand.

Hester differenced it back over two days. On the evening of the thirteenth she came to Dorset Street herself, with the proof and her sheets, and asked for Lady Lovelace and Mr Dunn together.

"Third differences," she said, and laid the sheet on the bench under the lamp. "Smooth from ninety-five to seventy-two. Here," and she put her finger on it, "at seventy-one, they jump. And then they come back smooth again from seventy, but on a different line. Like this." She drew it with her finger in the air, a stream with a stone in it. "The figure at seventy-one is wrong in the sixth place by one. And every figure after it carries the one."

Ada looked at the sheet. Then she looked at Enoch.

Enoch did not say anything. He went to the engine and took the lamp from the bench and held it close to the columns, and turned the crank back, very slowly, one turn at a time, counting, until the top column stood where it had stood when it printed the figure for age seventy-one. Then he took the cover off the carriage at the back of the sixth wheel and looked for a long time, and put his hand in, and took it out, and put a gauge in, and took it out, and said:

"The carry lever on the sixth wheel's worn. Here, at the nose. It's taken a carry it shouldn't, once, when the wheel above it was at nine and this one at nought. It'll not do it often. Only when the figures fall just so." He held the lever up in the lamplight, between finger and thumb. There was nothing to see, at first; and then Ada saw it, a bright flat where the steel had been rubbed by ten thousand turns of the crank, no wider than a hair. "It's in the Metal column, my lady. "It's a fault of somebody's."

"It's a fault of steel," Hester said. "That's what the Rule's for."

Ada wrote it in the green book that night. She wrote: Table I, annuities, Carlisle, 3 per cent. Printed 9th July 1850. Differenced by H.F.: discrepancy at age 71, sixth place, carried forward. Traced by E.D. to a worn carry lever, sixth wheel. Lever replaced. Table reprinted 16th July and differenced again and drawn by lot at twelve arguments by H.F., and found the same. Accepted for the trustees, G.D. And she initialled it and left a space beside her initials, and when Davies came on the seventeenth he wrote G.D. in it, and the Guardian printed the table in its tariff for 1851, and paid.

The Exhibition opened in Hyde Park on the first of May, 1851.

Babbage had not wanted to send the engine. He had quarrelled with the Royal Commission the year before over the arrangement of the classes, and had written a pamphlet against it, and said in the study that he would not put his engine among the mangles and the steam ploughs to be gawped at by excursionists from Leeds. Davies said that the Guardian wanted its engine computing and not standing in a glass house for six months. Enoch said the move would shake the frame out of true and he would have to set it again from the beginning. Ada said that the Commissioners had offered space in the Machinery Court, and that a machine which printed tables in public every afternoon for six months, before the whole of England and half of Europe, with a computer at a side table checking every page by the Rule in front of anyone who cared to watch, would answer Mr Airy's other question better than anything she could write.

"Whether it is wanted," said Babbage.

"Whether anyone believes it," said Ada. "That's the same question."

They sent it. Enoch set it up on its bed in the Machinery Court in April among the steam hammers and the power looms, under the great glass roof, and had it true again in eleven days. From the first of May it printed one page each afternoon at three o'clock, a page of annuities at a different rate each day, and the moulds were cast in a little furnace behind a rope, and a proof pulled on a hand press and pinned up on a board where the crowd could see it. At a table beside the board, with her back to the crowd, sat Hester, differencing the day's page by hand. When she had done it she wrote at the foot of the proof, in pencil, Differenced, H.F., and the date, and pinned it beside the first.

People watched her as much as they watched the engine. A newspaper called her the Lady Arithmetician, and Hester said nothing about it to anyone except Kate, who was seventeen and a pupil-teacher now, and thought it very fine.

Ada came on a morning in June before the doors opened to the shilling public, on a pass from the Commissioners, with William. She had been bleeding since April. She had told William, and Dr Locock, and no one else. Dr Locock had said it was a disorder of the womb, and had looked at her for a long time, and said that he would like to see her again in a month.

She walked down the long aisle of the Machinery Court on William's arm, slowly, past the locomotive and the hydraulic press and the cotton machines, and stopped in front of the engine. Enoch was there, early, oiling it. He took off his cap. Hester was not there yet.

"Will you turn it for me?" Ada said. "Not for the page. For me."

Enoch looked at the clock on the wall and then at her. He set the columns from the morning's figures and put his hand on the crank and turned it, slowly, and the long soft rattle went up under the glass roof, and the carriage lifted, all at once, and the type wheels moved, and the morning sun came in across the court in long bars full of dust and fell across the brass, and Ada stood and watched it with her hand on William's arm until a page was done.

"There," she said. "It's finished."

William said nothing. She felt his arm under her hand, steady, and was grateful for it, and for his saying nothing.

Dr Locock saw her again in July, and said the word, and she went home and told William, and her mother, and then, last, as she had once told William last, she told the green book, which she did not write in: she sat with it on her knee and did not open it.

The jurors awarded the engine a Council Medal in October. The medal was struck in the name of Charles Babbage alone. The jurors' report, which ran to three pages on the engine, named the Calculating Engine Subscription, and Mr Griffith Davies, F.R.S., and the Countess of Lovelace, who had conducted its business; it did not name the foreman who had made it true or the computer who had checked it every afternoon for five months and a half.

Ada read the report at Great Cumberland Place, in bed. She read it twice. Then she sent for Davies and asked him to bring the green book, and when he came she had him write in it, at her dictation, because her own hand that day was not to be trusted: The jurors have named the conductor. They have not named the foreman or the second hand. This book names them: Enoch Dunn, foreman, who made it true; Hester Fell, computer, who would not let it lie. And she took the pen from him and put her initials under it, very slowly, and then held the pen out to him, and he wrote G.D.

Babbage hung the medal in its case in the drawing room at Dorset Street, on the wall above where the engine had stood, and when people asked him about it he said that it was his engine and that the Commissioners had shown more sense than he had expected. But Enoch, who went to Dorset Street in November to take the engine back from Hyde Park, found that Mr Babbage had had a second card written and slipped into the case behind the first, where it could only be seen if one looked closely, in his own hand: With A.A.L., who would have it finished.","authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":41}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"draft","text":"ELEVEN: THE LAST ARTICLE

The engine went to Lombard Street in the second week of January, 1852, in nine crates on three drays, with Enoch walking beside the first dray the whole way from Dorset Street with one hand on the tailboard, as if it might otherwise get away from him. The Guardian had cleared a back room on the ground floor, behind the clerks' hall, where the floor had been taken up and a bed of brick and stone laid to Enoch's drawing, and by the end of the month the engine stood on it under a skylight, and printed, on the first of February, a table of joint lives at four per cent, which Hester differenced in Chalton Street and found smooth.

Ada did not see it there. She had not been out of Great Cumberland Place since November except to be driven in the park on fine days, wrapped to the chin, and in the new year the fine days stopped.

William had the account of it from Davies, who came on the third of February to tell her, and found her asleep, and told William instead in the library. Davies stood with his back to the fire and described the brick bed and the skylight and the joint-lives table in some detail, and then stopped, and looked at the carpet, and said that he hoped Lady Lovelace would know that the offices were very satisfied, and that the subscribers had voted to continue the subscription for the printing of further tables at the rate agreed, and that there was nothing else she need trouble herself with, nothing at all.

"I'll tell her," William said.

"Tell her nothing's withheld," said Davies. "She'll know what I mean."

The spring was bad and the summer was worse. William learned the names of things: the haemorrhages, the doses, Dr Locock's careful phrases, and later Dr West's, and later the mesmerist her mother brought, whom William disliked on sight and did not send away, because it was not his to send. Lady Byron had come up in March to take the house in hand and had taken it in hand. She decided who came up the stairs. Greig came, because he was Mrs Somerville's son and a lawyer, and De Morgan's wife came, and the children came at the hours appointed. Babbage did not come, after June. He came once in June and stayed an hour and Ada was so bright after it, and so ill the next day, that Lady Byron wrote to him that it would be better for her daughter if he did not come again, and he did not come again, and wrote instead, every few days, letters about the engine in Lombard Street that William read aloud to Ada when she could not hold them.

In August she asked William to send for Babbage, in spite of her mother, to ask him to be her executor. Babbage came, and went up, and came down after twenty minutes with a face William did not want to look at, and said in the hall, picking up his hat, that he had agreed, and that he supposed Lady Byron would not allow it, and that he would not contest it if she did not. Lady Byron did not allow it. Babbage did not contest it.

It was in the last week of August that Ada told William the thing that she told him.

He had been sitting with her in the afternoon. The blinds were half down against the heat. She had been quiet a long time and he had thought she was asleep, and then she said his name, and he went to the bed, and she told him.

This book does not know what she said. William never told anyone, and the people who have written since about what passed between them in that week have guessed, and their guesses do not agree, and a guess is not a figure. What is known is what he did. He stood up. He stood by the bed for a moment longer, and then he went out of the room, and down the stairs, and out of the front door into Great Cumberland Place, without his hat, and walked. He walked for most of the night. He came back at four in the morning and sat in the library until it was light, and at nine he went up again, because he had been told she was asking, and she was asleep when he got there, and he sat by the bed until she woke, and when she woke neither of them spoke of it.

He did not leave her again. But something had gone, and both of them knew it had gone, and it did not come back, and they were both too tired to pretend about it, and did not.

On the second of September she asked Greig to bring the green book from Dorset Street.

Greig brought it on the third. William was in the room. Greig gave it to Ada, who could not hold it, and he set it open on the bed-tray in front of her, at the next clear leaf, after the jurors' page with Davies's hand on it and the names of Enoch Dunn and Hester Fell. He had brought a pen and ink. He put the pen in her hand and closed her fingers on it.

She wrote very slowly. The hand wandered. Greig sat by the window, where he could not see the page, and William stood at the foot of the bed, where he could not see it either. It took her most of an hour. Twice she stopped and slept, with the pen still in her fingers, and Greig took it gently out and put it back when she woke.

When she had finished she asked Greig to read it aloud. Greig read it.

"Article the Last. That the husband who owns this book by law shall own it also by gift. That he shall read every page of it, including my mother's sheet. That he shall do with it what he thinks right after I am dead."

He stopped. There was nothing else on the page except her initials, A.A.L., and beside them the space.

William waited for her to ask him something; to forgive her, to sign, to say anything at all. She did not ask him anything. She looked at him across the bed for a while and then she shut her eyes.

Greig closed the book and gave it to William. William held it. It was heavier than he had thought it would be, because of all the things pasted in.

"Will you sign it?" Greig said quietly, in the passage outside, afterwards. "There's a space."

"No," said William. "She didn't ask me to."

"She left the space."

"She always leaves the space." He looked at the green cloth, worn pale at the corners. "It's for the other one to decide."

He took it down to the library and put it in the drawer of his desk and locked the drawer, and did not open it while she lived.

She lived until the twenty-seventh of November. The last weeks were very bad, and they are not told here, because they were hers and her mother's and the doctors', and the book has no articles for them. William was in the house when she died, in the evening, and was in the room, at the end, and held her hand, which he had held from the Strand to Charing Cross eight years before after signing the clause that said she did not exist in law, and which she had held then as far as Charing Cross and no farther, because that was as far as she held anything in public. She was thirty-six. It was a few days short of her birthday.

She was buried at Hucknall, in the Byron vault, beside her father, whom she had never seen, as she had asked. William went. Babbage did not; he was not asked. Davies sent a wreath from the Guardian. Hester Fell, in Chalton Street, heard of it from Enoch, who read it in the Times on the twenty-ninth and walked up from Lombard Street at his dinner hour to tell her, and stood in the doorway, and did not come in; and Hester sat at her table for a long time after he had gone, and then took a clean sheet and ruled a narrow margin down it, and sat looking at the margin, and did not write anything in it at all.

In December, at Horsley, when the house had emptied, William unlocked the drawer and took out the green book and sat down at the desk with it and opened it at the first leaf: The Book of Conditions. Between C.B. and A.A.L., with A. De M. as umpire. Every article to be initialled by both. Nothing binds that is not written here.

He began to read every page. It took him three evenings. On the third he came to her mother's sheet, in the small upright hand he knew, with A.I.N.B. beside it, and read it twice; and turned the leaf, and read the Rule of Two Hands; and the page about the jurors; and then the last page, with its wandering hand, and her initials, and the space beside them.

He sat with it open for a long time. Then he closed it, and put it back in the drawer, and locked it, and kept it, as she had said, and did with it what he thought right, which for twenty-five years was nothing at all.","authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":43}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"draft","text":"TWELVE: HORSLEY, 1878

The letter from Lord Lovelace came to Chalton Street in March, on paper with a coronet, asking whether Mrs Fell would do him the kindness of coming to Horsley on the fourth of April, by the train to Effingham Junction, where a carriage would meet her, to read some tables in a book that he wished to give to Major-General Babbage; and that he would be grateful to her, as the only person living who could tell him whether the tables were right.

Hester was sixty-seven. She still lived in the two rooms over the corn-chandler's, though the chandler was a different chandler and the stairs were harder than they had been. She still computed, three days a week, for the Guardian, which had given up its engine eleven years before and gone over, like every other office, to the new tables of the Institute of Actuaries, computed by hand by young men in a room in Chancery Lane, and checked, by a rule the Institute had adopted in 1866 and called the Rule of Two Hands without saying where it came from, by a second young man, or by a woman of sixty-seven in Somers Town at sixpence a page.

She went, because she was curious, and because she did not know what book he meant.

The carriage at Effingham was a closed landau with a coachman who said nothing for four miles. Horsley Towers, when they came to it, was a long flint house with a great many towers that did not seem to Hester to be holding anything up, and a hall with a timber roof like a church's. Lord Lovelace met her in the library. He was a tall old man, seventy-three, who walked with a stick and sat carefully, as if furniture were something one might damage, and he thanked her for coming in a voice that she remembered, though she had heard it only once before, in the Machinery Court, in June of 1851, saying nothing.

Major-General Babbage was there too, a man of fifty-three with his father's forehead and none of his father's restlessness, back from India these four years, who had the old engine now in the coach house at Dorset Street where it had been built, and his father's papers in forty-one boxes, and who said, shaking her hand, that he had read her name in his father's letters and had not expected to meet her.

Lord Lovelace had the book on the table. It was a green quarto with a leather spine, the cloth worn pale at the corners and gone grey along the fore-edge where hands had held it, swollen to half again its thickness with what had been pasted into it.

"My wife kept this," he said. "From the autumn of 1843. Everything she and Mr Babbage agreed is in it, and some things other people agreed. When she was dying she gave it to me. She asked me to read every page and to do with it what I thought right. I have read every page, more than once. I have done nothing with it, for twenty-five years, because I did not know what was right. I think now that it belongs with the engine, and the engine is Henry's." He touched the cover. "But there are tables in it. Copies of the first tables, and her working of the Rule. Before I give it away I should like to know that what is written in it is true. I'm told you are the person to ask."

"I am the person who checked them," Hester said. "I don't know about true."

He smiled for the first time. "That will do."

They left her alone with it, at the long table under the window, with a lamp and her own pencil and a ruled sheet she had brought in her bag from habit. It was a grey April afternoon with rain coming over the Downs.

She opened it at the first leaf. The Book of Conditions. Between C.B. and A.A.L., with A. De M. as umpire. Every article to be initialled by both. Nothing binds that is not written here. And inside the front board, in faded ink: 4s. 6d.

She had heard of the book for thirty years and never seen it. She read it from the beginning, slowly, not as a computer reads but as one reads a letter. Article the First, in pencil gone over in ink, with its four argued words. Mr Clement's memorandum under its gummed strip, which she lifted and read on both sides. What the law says I am, and under it, What this book says I am, initialled A.A.L. and C.B. Article the Third and Mr De Morgan's award, with the figure two hundred and eighty-four pounds six shillings, which she remembered Enoch working out on the back of a drawing. A sheet in a small upright hand, pasted, with three conditions on it and four initials beside it that she did not know.

And then the Rule of Two Hands, in Lady Lovelace's clearest writing, and under it, Mr Davies's G.D. for the trustees, and her ladyship's initials; and under those, in the same hand, smaller:

Proved on her own figures by Mrs Hester Fell, computer, of Chalton Street, who is the second hand.

Hester sat and looked at it for a long time.

Then she did what she had come to do. She turned to the copy of Table I, which Lady Lovelace had written out fair on two leaves, and took out her pencil and her ruled sheet, and differenced it back, as she had in 1850, all eighty-six figures, to the third order. It took her an hour and a half. The rain came and went. The third differences were smooth from ninety-five to ten, all the way down. Lady Lovelace had copied the reprinted table, not the first; the stone at seventy-one was not in it. The note beside it said so: Traced by E.D. to a worn carry lever, sixth wheel. Lever replaced.

She read the jurors' page, in Mr Davies's engraver's hand, and found her name a second time, written out whole beside Enoch's: Enoch Dunn, foreman, who made it true; Hester Fell, computer, who would not let it lie.

She put the pencil down.

She had not seen Enoch for twenty-five years. He had asked her to marry him on a Sunday in February 1853, walking back round the Regent's Park in a thin snow. Mr Whitworth had written to offer him a foremanship at Chorlton Street, the best place in the works, and he wanted to take it, and he wanted to take her with him, and Kate, who was nineteen and could teach anywhere. Hester had known for a year that he would ask, and had known for a year what she would say, and it had not made it easier to say.

She had told him plainly. She would not leave Kate, who was courting a compositor in Holborn and would not go north. She would not leave the work, which was the Guardian's work and the engine's and hers. And she would not marry, him or anyone: because the moment she married, her wages as the engine's second hand, the first money she had ever earned in her own right as more than a pair of hands at piecework, would by law be her husband's; and she had seen what it cost a countess to have to have a man sign for her in a lawyer's chambers before she could so much as be named in a schedule, and she was not a countess.

He had said he would never touch a penny of it.

She had said: I know you wouldn't. The law would.

He went north in April. They wrote for some years, every month at first, and then at Christmas. He had married, in 1861, a widow in Ardwick with two boys. She had written to wish him well and meant it. Kate had married her compositor in 1856 and had four children and a house in Kentish Town with a bay window, and came to Chalton Street on Sundays. In 1870 Parliament had passed an Act by which a married woman might keep her own earnings, and Hester had read it in the paper, at the window, and put the paper down, and gone on with the table she was checking, and had not thought about it again for a week, and then had thought about it for a long time.

So many of them were dead. Mr Davies in 1855, in March, at his desk, they said, with a pen in his hand. Lady Byron in 1860. Mr De Morgan in 1871, in March, broken by his son's death; and Mr Babbage in the October, in his house in Dorset Street, an old man who had gone on designing his Analytical Engine to the end, in drawings no one had initialled, and who had had the table engine brought back from Lombard Street in 1867 and set up again in the coach house where it was made, and had taken the medal down from the drawing room wall and hung it over the engine instead. Mrs Somerville in Naples in 1872, at ninety-one.

The light was going. Hester closed the table and turned to the last leaf.

Article the Last. The hand wandered across the page like the hand of someone writing in a moving carriage. That the husband who owns this book by law shall own it also by gift. That he shall read every page of it, including my mother's sheet. That he shall do with it what he thinks right after I am dead. A.A.L. And beside the initials, the space.

Every other article in the book was initialled twice. She turned back through it to be sure. Every one, twice, or three times, or four. This one, once.

Lord Lovelace came in at six with the lamp lit and Major-General Babbage behind him.

"Well, Mrs Fell?"

"The tables are right, my lord," Hester said. "I've differenced the first by hand. It's smooth all the way. The note beside it is right too. I was there." She hesitated. "My name's in it. Twice."

"Yes," he said. "She put it there. I've wondered whether you knew."

"I didn't know."

"No. I thought not." He came and stood by the table and looked down at the open book, at the last leaf. Hester saw where he was looking.

"There's a space, my lord," she said.

"There is."

"Every other one has two hands to it."

He stood for a while. Then he put his stick against the table and took a pen from the stand and dipped it, slowly, and bent, and wrote in the space beside his wife's initials, in a hand much steadier than hers, two letters: W.L. And under them, the date: 4th April 1878.

He laid the pen down and closed the book and held it out to Henry Babbage, who took it in both hands.

"Nothing binds that is not written here," Lord Lovelace said. "It took me twenty-five years to see that the article was a condition like the rest, and wanted the other party." He picked up his stick. "Mrs Fell, you'll stay to dinner. The train's not till nine."

She stayed. At dinner Henry Babbage asked her about the Rule, and she told him, and he said he meant to build a working piece of his father's other engine, the great one, the mill at least, before he died, and that if he did he would want it checked by someone who would not let it lie.

"I'm sixty-seven, sir," said Hester.

"So you are," said Henry Babbage. "So you are. I shall have to be quick."

The carriage took her to Effingham in the dark. On the train she sat by the window with her bag on her knee and the ruled sheet inside it, with the third differences of Table I down one side, eighty-six of them, and a narrow margin, and in the margin, all the way down, the nothing that meant she trusted it.","authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":45}}

"I am the person who checked them," Hester said. "I don't know about true."

He smiled for the first time. "That will do."

They left her alone with it, at the long table under the window, with a lamp and her own pencil and a ruled sheet she had brought in her bag from habit. It was a grey April afternoon with rain coming over the Downs.

She opened it at the first leaf. The Book of Conditions. Between C.B. and A.A.L., with A. De M. as umpire. Every article to be initialled by both. Nothing binds that is not written here. And inside the front board, in faded ink: 4s. 6d.

She had heard of the book for thirty years and never seen it. She read it from the beginning, slowly, not as a computer reads but as one reads a letter. Article the First, in pencil gone over in ink, with its four argued words. Mr Clement's memorandum under its gummed strip, which she lifted and read on both sides. What the law says I am, and under it, What this book says I am, initialled A.A.L. and C.B. Article the Third and Mr De Morgan's award, with the figure two hundred and eighty-four pounds six shillings, which she remembered Enoch working out on the back of a drawing. A sheet in a small upright hand, pasted, with three conditions on it and four initials beside it that she did not know.

And then the Rule of Two Hands, in Lady Lovelace's clearest writing, and under it, Mr Davies's G.D. for the trustees, and her ladyship's initials; and under those, in the same hand, smaller:

Proved on her own figures by Mrs Hester Fell, computer, of Chalton Street, who is the second hand.

Hester sat and looked at it for a long time.

Then she did what she had come to do. She turned to the copy of Table I, which Lady Lovelace had written out fair on two leaves, and took out her pencil and her ruled sheet, and differenced it back, as she had in 1850, all eighty-six figures, to the third order. It took her an hour and a half. The rain came and went. The third differences were smooth from ninety-five to ten, all the way down. Lady Lovelace had copied the reprinted table, not the first; the stone at seventy-one was not in it. The note beside it said so: Traced by E.D. to a worn carry lever, sixth wheel. Lever replaced.

She read the jurors' page, in Mr Davies's engraver's hand, and found her name a second time, written out whole beside Enoch's: Enoch Dunn, foreman, who made it true; Hester Fell, computer, who would not let it lie.

She put the pencil down.

She had not seen Enoch for twenty-five years. He had asked her to marry him on a Sunday in February 1853, walking back round the Regent's Park in a thin snow. Mr Whitworth had written to offer him a foremanship at Chorlton Street, the best place in the works, and he wanted to take it, and he wanted to take her with him, and Kate, who was nineteen and could teach anywhere. Hester had known for a year that he would ask, and had known for a year what she would say, and it had not made it easier to say.

She had told him plainly. She would not leave Kate, who was courting a compositor in Holborn and would not go north. She would not leave the work, which was the Guardian's work and the engine's and hers. And she would not marry, him or anyone: because the moment she married, her wages as the engine's second hand, the first money she had ever earned in her own right as more than a pair of hands at piecework, would by law be her husband's; and she had seen what it cost a countess to have to have a man sign for her in a lawyer's chambers before she could so much as be named in a schedule, and she was not a countess.

He had said he would never touch a penny of it.

She had said: I know you wouldn't. The law would.

He went north in April. They wrote for some years, every month at first, and then at Christmas, and his letters were always about the shop, the gauges, the new rifled guns Mr Whitworth was making for the War Office, and never about anything else, and she read them at the window and understood them perfectly. Kate had married her compositor in 1856 and had four children and a house in Kentish Town with a bay window, and came to Chalton Street on Sundays. In 1870 Parliament had passed an Act by which a married woman might keep her own earnings, and Hester had read it in the paper, at the window, and put the paper down, and gone on with the table she was checking, and had not thought about it again for a week, and then had thought about it for a long time.

So many of them were dead. Mr Davies in 1855, in March, at his desk, they said, with a pen in his hand. Lady Byron in 1860. Mr De Morgan in 1871, in March, broken by his son's death; and Mr Babbage in the October, in his house in Dorset Street, an old man who had gone on designing his Analytical Engine to the end, in drawings no one had initialled, and who had had the table engine brought back from Lombard Street in 1867 and set up again in the coach house where it was made, and had taken the medal down from the drawing room wall and hung it over the engine instead. Mrs Somerville in Naples in 1872, at ninety-one.

The light was going. Hester closed the table and turned to the last leaf.

Article the Last. The hand wandered across the page like the hand of someone writing in a moving carriage. That the husband who owns this book by law shall own it also by gift. That he shall read every page of it, including my mother's sheet. That he shall do with it what he thinks right after I am dead. A.A.L. And beside the initials, the space.

Every other article in the book was initialled twice. She turned back through it to be sure. Every one, twice, or three times, or four. This one, once.

Lord Lovelace came in at six with the lamp lit and Major-General Babbage behind him.

"Well, Mrs Fell?"

"The tables are right, my lord," Hester said. "I've differenced the first by hand. It's smooth all the way. The note beside it is right too. I was there." She hesitated. "My name's in it. Twice."

"Yes," he said. "She put it there. I've wondered whether you knew."

"I didn't know."

"No. I thought not." He came and stood by the table and looked down at the open book, at the last leaf. Hester saw where he was looking.

"There's a space, my lord," she said.

"There is."

"Every other one has two hands to it."

He stood for a while. Then he put his stick against the table and took a pen from the stand and dipped it, slowly, and bent, and wrote in the space beside his wife's initials, in a hand much steadier than hers, two letters: W.L. And under them, the date: 4th April 1878.

He laid the pen down and closed the book and held it out to Henry Babbage, who took it in both hands.

"Nothing binds that is not written here," Lord Lovelace said. "It took me twenty-five years to see that the article was a condition like the rest, and wanted the other party." He picked up his stick. "Mrs Fell, you'll stay to dinner. The train's not till nine."

She stayed. At dinner Henry Babbage asked her about the Rule, and she told him, and he said he meant to build a working piece of his father's other engine, the great one, the mill at least, before he died, and that if he did he would want it checked by someone who would not let it lie.

"I'm sixty-seven, sir," said Hester.

"So you are," said Henry Babbage. "So you are. I shall have to be quick."

The carriage took her to Effingham in the dark. On the train she sat by the window with her bag on her knee and the ruled sheet inside it, with the third differences of Table I down one side, eighty-six of them, and a narrow margin, and in the margin, all the way down, the nothing that meant she trusted it.

THREE: PROSPECT PLACE

Her first act of business was to cross the river.

She went on a Tuesday in the second week of January, 1844, in a hired brougham because she did not want the Lovelace arms on the door in Newington. William offered to come. She said that a man who had been called a thief by Mr Babbage for ten years would talk more freely to a woman alone, and William, who did not follow this, let her go.

Prospect Place was a row of brick houses off the Kent Road, and number twenty-one had a yard behind it and a long shed of blackened timber with skylights, and the noise of the shed came through the house as a steady grinding under everything, so that when the girl showed her into the front parlour the ornaments on the mantel were very slightly moving. Joseph Clement came in a few minutes later in a dressing gown over his waistcoat. He was sixty-four. He had been a weaver and a slater in Westmorland before he was a draughtsman, and he still had the shoulders of a man who carried slates, but he breathed as if each breath had to be fetched from a distance.

"Lady Lovelace," he said. "I have never had a countess in this room. I have had a great many lawyers."

"I have not come with a lawyer."

"No. You've come from him." He sat, carefully. "Sit down. You'll forgive me if I don't stand long."

She had decided in the carriage how to begin and she began that way. She told him that there was to be a new engine, smaller than the old one, made to a frozen design, for the life offices, and paid for by subscription and not by the Treasury. She told him there was a book in which every condition between herself and Mr Babbage was written, and an umpire. She did not tell him that only three articles were in it yet.

Clement listened with his head on one side, the way, she thought later, a man listens to a lathe to hear if the tool is cutting true.

"And what do you want of me?"

"Two things. The drawings of the old engine that are still here. Mr Babbage says they are his. You say, or your lawyers say, they are yours. I do not want to know who is right. I want to know whether he may come and copy them."

"And?"

"Your great planing machine. I want to know whether it can be bought."

He laughed at that, and the laugh became a cough, and the cough went on for some time. The girl came to the door and he waved her away.

"That planer," he said when he could, "has paid for this house twice. I take eighteen shillings a day for the use of it, and there's not another in London that'll give you a plane like it on a bed eight foot long. You know why I have it? Because his engine needed it. He wanted his frames true to a thousandth and nobody in England could make them so, so I made the machine that could, and when we fell out he said the machine was his because it was made for his work, and I said it was mine because it was made by my hands, and by the custom of the trade a man keeps the tools he makes. Every engineer in London knows that. Ask Whitworth. Whitworth worked in that shed."

"I don't dispute it."

"No. You want to buy it." He looked at her. "Who would be buying it? Not him."

"The trust. There will be a trust. I am trying to make sure there is nothing in this engine that anyone can say belongs to Mr Babbage alone, or to you alone, or to me."

"To you." He considered that. "What does a married lady own, in law?"

"Nothing," Ada said. "That is one reason it will be a trust."

He was quiet for a while. The grinding in the shed changed its note and then went back.

"I'm not going to live long," he said. "The doctor says the heart. I've no children. My brother's in Westmorland and would sell the planer to the first man who asked, and the first man who asked would be some railway shop that would run it into the ground in five years cutting rails. If your trust wants it, it can have it when I'm gone, at a fair price, and my executor can name the price. I'll write that down for you. As for the drawings, he can come and copy them. He can't take them away. They stay in this house till they go to my executor with everything else. Is that clear enough for your book?"

"Yes."

"Write it in, then." He leaned back. "Now I'll tell you something, since you've come so far. You'll have been told it was money. That the Treasury wouldn't pay my bills and I stopped work. It wasn't money. Money's never the reason a thing stops. Money's the reason given."

She waited.

"He would not stop changing it," Clement said. "Every week a new drawing. Every week a part we'd cut and fitted was wrong because the drawing it was cut to was wrong now. Not wrong. Improved. I've had men stand at the bench with a finished piece in their hands and nothing to do with it, because it belonged to last month's engine. You can't build to a man who thinks faster than metal can be cut. I told him so. He thought I was asking for more money. Maybe I was. A man must be paid for his idle hands as well as his busy ones." He shut his eyes for a moment. "I liked him. You'll not believe that. I liked him better than any man I ever worked for. He was the only one who ever understood what I was doing. That's why it was so bad."

Ada said, "In the book there is a blank article. It says that no part of the design may be altered after metal is cut for it, without the umpire's consent."

Clement opened his eyes.

"Has he signed it?"

"Not yet."

"Then get him to sign it," Clement said, "before you cut anything. That's my advice and you can have it for nothing."

He wrote his memorandum at a little table by the window, slowly, in a square tradesman's hand: that on his death his planing machine should be offered first to the trustees of the engine at a price to be fixed by his executor, and that Mr Babbage might copy at No. 21 Prospect Place such drawings of the former engine as were in Clement's keeping, but remove none. He signed it Jos. Clement and dated it, and blotted it, and handed it to her.

"Mind," he said, "you'll want a foreman who'll stand up to him. Not a gentleman. A man who'll stop the shop."

"Do you know one?"

"I know a few. They're all at Whitworth's." He almost smiled. "Ask Joe Whitworth to lend you one. He owes me a favour, though he'd not say so."

She drove back over Blackfriars Bridge in the early dark. The river was low and the lamps on the bridge were lit and the carriage wheels drummed on the granite setts. She held the memorandum in her lap in its fold. It was the first paper in the business that was not between herself and Babbage, and the first that had been signed by someone who would not be alive to see it honoured. She thought about the grinding in the shed, which she could still hear, faintly, as one hears the sea after leaving it.

That night she pasted the memorandum onto the fourth leaf of the green book, with a strip of gummed paper along the top edge so that it could be lifted and read on both sides, and under it she wrote: Received of Mr Clement, at Prospect Place, 9th January 1844. And under that: Article the Third remains to be initialled.

Babbage went to Prospect Place on the thirtieth of January to copy the drawings, with a draughtsman and a portfolio. He came back and wrote to Ada that Clement had been civil, that they had not quarrelled, and that the drawings were in a shocking state of disorder. He did not say whether they had shaken hands. She did not ask.

Joseph Clement died on the twenty-eighth of February. Babbage did not go to the funeral. He sent a note to the widow of Clement's brother, who had come down from Westmorland, and he sent, by Ada's arrangement and at her suggestion, a wreath in the name of the engine's trustees, though the engine had as yet no trustees and no name.

Some days afterwards she found Babbage in the study at Dorset Street with the green book open at the blank third article. He did not hear her come in. He was not reading it. He was looking at it the way she had seen him look at a drawing he meant to alter, and then he closed the book without writing anything and saw her and said, quite naturally, that the weather was very raw for March.
